{{Short description|Mathematical mapping between objects arising from their definitions}}
{{dablink|For the canonical map of an algebraic variety into projective space, see {{section link|Canonical bundle#Canonical maps}}.}}

In [[mathematics]], a '''canonical map''', also called a '''natural map''', is a [[Map (mathematics)|map]] or [[morphism]] between objects that arises naturally from the definition or the construction of the objects. Often, it is a map which preserves the widest amount of structure.<!-- and it tends to be unique. In the rare cases where latitude in choices remains, the map is either conventionally agreed upon to be the most useful for further analysis, or sometimes the most elegant map known to date.--> A choice of a canonical map sometimes depends on a convention (e.g., a sign convention).

A closely related notion is that of a '''structure map''' or '''structure morphism''': the map or morphism that comes with the given structure on the object. These are also sometimes called canonical maps.

A [[canonical isomorphism]] is a canonical map that is also an [[isomorphism]] (that is, [[Inverse function|invertible]]). In some contexts, it might be necessary to address an issue of ''choices'' of canonical maps or canonical isomorphisms; for a typical example, see [[prestack#Definition|prestack]].

==Examples==
*If {{mvar|N}} is a [[normal subgroup]] of a [[Group (mathematics)|group]] {{mvar|G}}, then there is a canonical [[surjective]] [[group homomorphism]] from {{mvar|G}} to the [[quotient group]] {{math|''G'' / ''N''}}, that sends an element {{mvar|g}} to the [[coset]] determined by {{mvar|g}}.
*If {{mvar|I}} is an [[ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] of a [[Ring (mathematics)|ring]] {{mvar|R}}, then there is a canonical surjective [[ring homomorphism]] from {{mvar|R}} onto the [[quotient ring]] {{math|''R'' / ''I''}} that sends an element {{mvar|r}} to its coset {{math|''I'' + ''r''}}.
*If {{mvar|S}} is a multiplicative set in commutative ring {{mvar|R}}, then there is a canonical ring homomorphism from {{mvar|R}} to the [[Localization (commutative algebra)|localization]] {{math|''S''<sup>−1</sup>''R''}} that sends element {{mvar|r}} to {{math|''r''/1}} in the localization. 
*If {{math|''R''<sub>''f''</sub>}} is the localization of commutative ring {{mvar|R}} by {{math|1=''S'' = {1, ''f'', ''f''<sup> 2</sup>, ''f''<sup> 3</sup>, ...<nowiki>}</nowiki>}}, and {{math|''R''<sub>p</sub>}} is the localization of {{mvar|R}} by {{math|1=''S'' = ''R'' \ p}}, where {{math|p}} is a prime ideal such that {{math|''f'' &notin; p}}, there is a canonical ring homomorphism {{math|α : ''R''<sub>''f''</sub> &rarr; ''R''<sub>p</sub>}} mapping {{math|''a''/''f''<sup>'' n''</sup>}} as an element of {{math|''R''<sub>''f''</sub>}} to {{math|''a''/''f''<sup>'' n''</sup>}} as an element of {{math|''R''<sub>p</sub>}}. If φ is the canonical map {{math|''R'' &rarr; ''R''<sub>p</sub>}} and ψ is the canonical map {{math|''R'' &rarr; ''R''<sub>''f''</sub>}}, then α is the unique map such that {{math|1=φ = α &compfn; ψ}}.
*If {{mvar|V}} is a finite-dimenstional [[vector space]], then there is a canonical map from {{mvar|V}} to the second [[dual space]] of {{mvar|V}}, that sends a vector {{mvar|v}} to the [[Linear form|linear functional]] {{mvar|f<sub>v</sub>}} defined by {{math|1=''f<sub>v</sub>''(λ) = λ(''v'')}}.
*If {{math|''f'': ''R'' → ''S''}} is a homomorphism between [[commutative ring]]s, then {{mvar|S}} can be viewed as an [[algebra over a ring|algebra]] over {{mvar|R}}. The ring homomorphism {{mvar|f}} is then called the structure map (for the algebra structure). The corresponding map on the [[prime spectrum|prime spectra]] {{math|''f<sup> *</sup>'': Spec(''S'') → Spec(''R'')}} is also called the structure map. More generally, a [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]] ''X'' over a scheme ''S'' is one equipped with a structure [[morphism of schemes|morphism]] {{math|''X'' &rarr; ''S''}}; for a scheme over a field ''k'' (e.g., a [[algebraic variety|variety]]), this is a morphism {{math|''X'' &rarr; Spec(''k'')}}.
*If {{mvar|E}} is a [[vector bundle]] over a [[topological space]] {{mvar|X}}, then the projection map from {{mvar|E}} to {{mvar|X}} is the structure map.
*In [[topology]], a canonical map is a function {{mvar|f}} mapping a set {{math|''X'' → ''X'' / ''R''}} ({{math|''X'' [[Modulo (mathematics)|mod]] ''R''}}), where {{mvar|R}} is an equivalence relation on {{mvar|X}}, that takes each {{mvar|x}} in {{mvar|X}} to the [[equivalence class]] {{math|[''x''] mod ''R''}}.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Eq4UDgAAQBAJ&pg=PA274|title=Handbook of Mathematics|last=Vialar|first=Thierry|date=2016-12-07|publisher=BoD - Books on Demand|isbn=9782955199008|language=en|pages=274}}</ref>
